opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
In the Gospel of John, Jesus says something that at first sounds almost blunt:

“Unless you people see signs and wonders, you will not believe.” — John 4:48

He says this to a royal official whose son is dying. The man has come desperately seeking help, hoping Jesus will come with him and heal the boy. Like many others who were following Jesus at the time, he is looking for a miracle, for something visible that will prove who Jesus is.

This moment reveals something deeply human about faith. People often want proof first. They want something dramatic, something unmistakable—something they can see before they will believe.

But in the Gospel of John, miracles are called signs. A sign is not meant to be the main event. A sign points to something beyond itself. The miracle is meant to reveal who Jesus is, not simply to amaze those who witness it.

In this moment, Jesus does something unexpected. Instead of going with the man or performing the miracle in front of him, He simply says:

“You may go; your son will live.” — John 4:50

No spectacle. No visible proof. Just a word.

The Gospel then records something very important: the man believed the word that Jesus spoke and began the journey home. At that moment he had not yet seen the miracle. He had only the word of Christ.

Later, as he travels home, his servants meet him on the road and tell him that his son has recovered. When he asks when the child began to improve, he realizes it was the exact moment Jesus spoke the words: “Your son will live.”

In that moment the man—and his entire household—comes to believe.

The story quietly teaches something profound about faith. Many people want belief to come after certainty, after signs, after visible proof. Yet the deeper movement of faith often happens the other way around. Trust begins with the word of Christ, even before the sign appears.

This is why later Jesus will say:

“Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.” — John 20:29

The line “Unless you people see signs and wonders, you will not believe” is not only a criticism. It is also an invitation. It invites a person to move beyond the need for constant proof and to begin trusting the voice of God itself. Faith grows not only from what we see, but from the willingness to trust the word spoken to us—even before the miracle becomes visible.
